try_it.prompt: Leo rolls two dice 36 times and gets 0 sevens. Using the rule on the card, what should he write under what happened?
try_it.answer: Zero is inside the doubt rule of 0 or 1 sevens. He should write that he got 0 sevens and that he now doubts the model. Next he could check the dice and roll again.

talk: Why should you write your doubt rule before you roll, not after?
Maya and Leo got 3 sevens, not 6. Why is that not enough to call the dice unfair?
If four friends each roll two dice 36 times, will they all get the same number of sevens? Why not?

check.question: Which of these is a testable prediction?
options: In 36 rolls of two fair dice, we will get about 6 sevens.
check.explanation: This prediction gives a number that a test can check. If the count were very far from 6, the test would make us doubt the model.

check.question: Your doubt rule is 0 or 1 sevens, or 12 or more. You roll 36 times and get 9 sevens. What should you do?
options: Change the rule so 9 counts as too many
Throw out the rolls and start over
Write down 9 sevens and say there is no reason to doubt the dice yet
check.explanation: Nine is not past either line of your rule, so you keep the model for now. Changing the rule after you see the result would not be a fair test.

check.question: Remember Lesson 5. Why do scientists flip a coin to choose who goes in which group?
options: So the groups always have exactly equal averages
So no person can steer the strong ones into one group
check.explanation: A coin does not take sides, so hidden differences balance out on average. It does not promise exactly equal groups every time.

lessons.connect: Careful scientists often write down their predictions and doubt rules before they collect data. Then nobody can move the line after seeing the results. You can write a model card for any test, from dice to paper planes.

grownups.why: The Common Core asks students to build a probability model, here 36 equally likely ordered pairs, and to compare its predictions with observed frequencies, explaining possible reasons for a mismatch (7.SP.7) [@ccss_math]. OpenStax defines equally likely outcomes and relative frequency, and states the law of large numbers: the relative frequency tends toward the theoretical probability as the number of trials grows, so a short run of 36 rolls can still land some way off [@openstax_prob]. The NGSS practices ask children to make predictions, plan investigations, and use evidence to judge an explanation [@ngss_appf]. The doubt rule of 0 or 1 sevens, or 12 or more, is a two-sided cutoff: with fair dice, the binomial chance of a count that far off in 36 rolls is about 0.023. The roll sequence comes from the course's seeded random number generator (seed 1), so the 3 sevens in the story, the video and this guide match.
misconceptions: If the count is not exactly 6, the model is wrong. (Counts vary; 3 sevens in 36 rolls is not unusual for fair dice.)
A test that agrees with the model proves it is true. (It only means the test gave no reason to doubt it; a later test still could.)
It is fine to choose the doubt rule after seeing the results. (Choosing it afterward lets you excuse any result; set it in advance.)
A sum of 7 has one way to happen, 3 and 4. (Order matters on two dice: 3 then 4 and 4 then 3 are different pairs, so there are 6 ways.)
grownups.simplify: Use 18 rolls and predict about 3 sevens. Skip the doubt rule numbers and simply ask: would 0 sevens surprise you?
grownups.extend: Pool the 36-roll tallies from several people. Plot how many sevens each person got, and see that most counts land between 3 and 9. Then write a model card for the sum of 2, which has a chance of 1 out of 36.

lessons.caution: Passing a test does not prove a model is true, and one unusual result does not prove it false. About 2 times in 100, fair dice will break this doubt rule by chance alone.

unit.big_question: How do we describe chance, test fairly, and tell what waves can do that coins cannot?
unit.summary: Learners turn counts into fractions and probabilities, compare what a model predicts with what really happens, and use random assignment to make a fair comparison. Then they meet waves, which can add up or cancel. That idea, adding first and then squaring, is the first step toward quantum physics.
unit.for_whom: Learners aged about 9 to 12 who have finished Level 0 or can count, compare, and read simple tables. They can work through most of a lesson alone. A grown-up or teacher checks the record sheet and joins the talk questions.

time.pace: Two lessons a week takes about six weeks, including the final project. Any lesson can be split into two sittings: story, animation and activity one day, practice and checks the next.

session_flow: Warm up: answer the look-back question from memory.
Read the story and watch the animation.
Do the hands-on activity and keep a record.
Practice together, then try two on your own.
Talk about it, then answer the three check questions. Say or write your answer before you open it.
Grown-ups: read the short guide at the end of the page.

outcomes.text: I can write a fraction from a count and use it to describe part of a group.
I can build a probability model and find the probability of an event and of its opposite.
I can tell a probability apart from a frequency, and explain why more trials help.
I can find a probability inside a group by using the right total.
I can explain how random assignment makes a comparison fair.
I can draw a common-cause diagram for two things that go up and down together.
I can describe a wave and explain how two waves can add up or cancel.
I can explain why not knowing a hidden result is different from the two-path experiment with light, and write a model that a test could prove wrong.

unit.evidence: Progress shows up three ways. Each lesson ends with three check questions. From Lesson 2 on, one of them looks back at an earlier lesson. Each activity produces a record (a table, a graph, or a diagram) that a grown-up can look at. The final project uses a four-part checklist.
materials: Two coins, two dice, and a paper cup
Counters, beads, or building bricks in two or three colors, and a paper bag
Graph paper or a printed grid, a ruler, pencils, and colored pencils
A calculator (optional)
A jump rope or a long, soft rope, or a toy spring coil
A shallow tray or baking dish of water and a small cup
Paper for paper airplanes or a paper cup tower, and masking tape
unit.safety: Keep coins, dice, and small counters away from babies and toddlers. Use water trays on a towel, away from screens and plugs, and wipe up spills right away. Swing ropes slowly, with space around you.

project.title: My chance and cause investigation
project.summary: Over three sittings, the learner runs a small experiment with random assignment, compares a model with real counts, and writes a model card.
questions: Does a paper airplane with folded wing tips fly farther than one without? Flip a coin to decide which plane each throw uses.
Do two dice add to 7 as often as a model predicts?
Does a ball roll farther on carpet or on a hard floor? Use a coin to decide the order of the trials.
steps: Pick a question. Write a prediction and the model behind it.
Plan a fair test. Use a coin or a die to assign which choice each trial gets.
Run at least 20 trials. Record every result in a table.
Turn your counts into fractions, and compare them with your model.
Make a graph of your results.
Write a model card: question, assumptions, prediction, what would prove it wrong, and what happened.

rubric.got: I wrote a question and a prediction from a model.
rubric.explain: I can say what my model assumes.

rubric.got: I used a coin or die to assign the choices.
rubric.explain: I can say why random assignment makes it fair.

rubric.got: I recorded at least 20 trials and turned them into fractions.
rubric.explain: I can say why my fractions are not exactly what the model predicted.

rubric.got: I compared my results with my prediction.
rubric.explain: I named a result that would have proved my model wrong.

project.safety: Throw paper airplanes away from faces. Roll balls away from stairs. Keep dice away from babies and toddlers.

udl: Each story comes with an animation and a written description of what it shows.
Learners can show what they know in a table, a graph, a drawing, or by explaining aloud.
Each lesson has a way to make it easier and a way to make it harder.
Activities use cheap household things, and the animations play without sound.

standards.text: Plan and conduct fair tests in which variables are controlled and the number of trials considered.
Develop a model of waves to describe patterns in terms of amplitude and wavelength.
Understand a fraction 1/b as one part of a whole cut into b equal parts.
Explain why two fractions are equivalent, using visual fraction models.
Recognize a statistical question as one that expects variability in the data.
Probability as a number from 0 to 1; approximate it from data; build and compare probability models.

unit.approach: Like Level 0, this unit was planned backward from its outcomes [@ubd_whitepaper], and each lesson moves from recall, to an example, to doing, to talking it through [@merrill2002], with built-in retrieval and spaced review [@dunlosky2013]. New in Level 1, each lesson has a short animation made with Manim Community Edition, an open-source animation library forked from the tool Grant Sanderson created for his 3Blue1Brown videos [@manim_ce]. The animations use the course's own tested simulation code, so the numbers on screen match the text. The probability ideas follow OpenStax Introductory Statistics [@openstax_prob; @openstax_design]; the wave ideas follow OpenStax Physics [@openstax_waves; @openstax_interference].
